summary: For ages 9–11: many animals think, learn, and have complex social lives — tool use (chimps, New Caledonian crows), self-recognition in the mirror mark test (dolphins, with magpies and elephants as debated cases, because later studies have not always repeated the results), problem-solving (octopuses), teaching young (meerkats), and apparent grief (elephants). The load-bearing idea is the EVIDENCE question: how do we actually know an animal thinks, how do scientists test it, and how do we avoid reading human feelings into animals (anthropomorphism) by ruling out simpler explanations like instinct or trial-and-error. A key concept is that intelligence takes different, life-fitted forms across species rather than a single ladder with humans on top.
misconceptions: 'Animals just act on instinct and can't really think or learn' — many show flexible problem-solving, learning, and teaching.
'Intelligence is a single ladder with humans at the top and others below' — intelligence takes different forms suited to each species' life.
'If an animal looks like it feels what we'd feel, it definitely does' (anthropomorphism) — scientists require evidence and rule out simpler explanations.
'Passing/failing the mirror test proves an animal is/ isn't intelligent overall' — it tests one specific ability (self-recognition), not intelligence in general.
'Only mammals are intelligent' — birds (crows), cephalopods (octopuses), and others show remarkable cognition.

activities.title: How do you KNOW? Questioning a cognition scientist
steps: Pick a clever animal behaviour to discuss — an elephant that seems to mourn, a crow bending a wire into a hook, a dolphin at a mirror.
Describe what is actually observed (not what you assume the animal feels).

Face the challenge question: 'That's what it looks like to us — but how could we test whether the animal understands, or whether it's trial-and-error, or whether we're just seeing our own feelings in it?'
Propose a concrete test: mark the animal and show it a mirror; give it a puzzle it could not have been born knowing how to solve.
State what a single positive result shows (one specific ability) and what it does NOT show (general intelligence).
activities.insight: Separating evidence from assumption is the scientific habit here: a behaviour that looks like a human feeling needs a designed test and the ruling-out of simpler explanations before we claim an animal understands.

activities.title: Test the mind: running and interpreting experiments
steps: Run a mirror mark test on a species: place a mark the animal cannot feel where it cannot see it directly, present the mirror, and observe whether the animal uses the reflection to investigate the mark on its own body more than it touches that spot without the mirror.
Run a puzzle box or multi-step problem on a different species and watch how it works out a solution.
Record a conclusion for each test: what ability the result demonstrates, and what it does not.
Sort behaviours into 'evidence' (what the behaviour actually shows) versus 'assumption' (what we merely imagine the animal feels).
Meet a trick scenario where trial-and-error or luck mimics insight, and decide what further evidence you would demand before concluding the animal 'understands'.
activities.insight: Each test probes one specific ability; a result must be interpreted carefully, and apparent insight can sometimes be explained by simpler processes unless further evidence rules them out.

activities.title: Different kinds of clever — not one ladder
steps: Gather varied examples across tool use (chimp, crow), problem-solving (octopus opening a jar, escaping a tank), memory, communication, social learning and teaching (meerkats teaching pups to handle scorpions), and self-recognition (dolphin, plus the debated magpie and elephant cases).
Match each animal to the kind of intelligence it shows, and to the way its own life makes that ability useful.
Compare an octopus, a crow, and a dolphin and explain how each is clever in a different, life-fitted way.
Answer: a pigeon has a tiny brain but can recognise hundreds of pictures — does brain size decide intelligence? Give a reason.
Explain why ranking species on a single 'smartness' line below humans is the wrong model.
activities.insight: Intelligence takes different forms suited to each species' life; it is not a single ladder with humans at the top, and brain size alone does not decide it.

checkQuestion: An octopus can open a jar to reach food and squeeze out of its tank to escape, but it can't do many things a chimpanzee can. Does that make the octopus 'less intelligent' than the chimp — or is that the wrong way to think about it? Explain your reasoning.
checkAnswer: Ranking them on one ladder is the wrong way. Intelligence takes different forms suited to each animal's life. An octopus is brilliant at solving physical puzzles, changing colour and escaping with its boneless body; a chimp is skilled with tools and in a complex social group. Each is highly intelligent in the ways its own survival needs, so you can't simply say one is 'smarter' overall — they are intelligent in different ways.
